entities.name: Cephisodotus the Elder
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cephisodotus the Elder, an Athenian sculptor active in the late 5th century BCE, holds a significant, albeit somewhat elusive, position in the history of Classical Greek art. While his individual works are largely unconfirmed and often conflated with those of his son, Praxiteles, or a later sculptor of the same name (Cephisodotus the Younger), his primary importance stems from his role as the progenitor of a distinguished artistic lineage. He represents a transitional figure, working in the waning years of the High Classical period, an era defined by the Parthenon's idealism and the burgeoning humanism that would characterize the 4th century BCE.

Operating within the vibrant artistic hub of Athens during the aftermath of the Peloponnesian War, Cephisodotus is believed to have contributed to the stylistic evolution from the severe solemnity of earlier High Classical sculpture towards a greater naturalism and emotional nuance. Though no securely attributed works survive, ancient sources suggest he was a skilled craftsman, laying the groundwork for the more expressive and graceful forms that his son, Praxiteles, would later perfect. His commissions likely involved public monuments and cult statues, typical of Athenian artistic production, reflecting the city-state's enduring civic and religious life even amidst political upheaval.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cephisodotus the Elder's significance primarily lies in his role as the father and likely first teacher of Praxiteles, one of the most celebrated sculptors of the 4th century BCE, thereby establishing a crucial artistic lineage. His work, though largely unconfirmed, contributed to the stylistic evolution of Greek sculpture towards greater naturalism.
